title: Lula has won in Brazil, but Europe still needs to fight for Mercosur – European Council on Foreign Relations
gist: Rizzi argues Lula's fourth-term win in Brazil should rescue the EU-Mercosur deal, but Brussels must still secure European Parliament approval and back it with money, because the deal is key to accessing Brazil's lithium and graphite. China dominates Brazil's green-tech imports and is courting investment, while Brazil's push for local value added favours European firms that build local supply chains.

insights.claim: Lula secured an unprecedented fourth term as Brazil's president in the October 25th 2026 run-off against Flávio Bolsonaro, a comeback after trailing in the first round.
insights.speaker: Alberto Rizzi
insights.so_what: Removes the worst-case scenario for the EU-Mercosur deal.

insights.claim: Lula's win does not finish the job: the European Parliament still needs to approve the EU-Mercosur agreement in a plenary vote before national ratification, and to give legitimacy to its provisional implementation.
insights.speaker: Alberto Rizzi
insights.so_what: Parliament plenary vote is the next binary catalyst for EU-Mercosur trade exposure.

insights.claim: Trump has cast doubt over the Brazilian result and Bolsonaro vows to challenge it in court, although Brazil has no precedent for overturning an election win.
insights.speaker: Alberto Rizzi
insights.so_what: Post-election legal challenge adds noise but low probability of overturn.

insights.claim: Brazil's fragmented Congress is likely to limit Lula's room for manoeuvre.
insights.speaker: Alberto Rizzi
insights.so_what: Expect constrained domestic policy delivery in Brazil despite a pro-EU president.
insights.quote: But Brazil’s fragmented Congress is likely to limit Lula’s room for manoeuvre.

insights.claim: Bolsonaro appeared willing to grant the US preferential treatment on government contracts and access to Brazil's mineral resources, whereas Lula has driven the EU-Mercosur deal.
insights.speaker: Alberto Rizzi
insights.so_what: Lula's win tilts Brazilian mineral access towards Europe rather than the US.

insights.claim: The Mercosur deal is instrumental in securing European access to Brazil's critical minerals, including lithium and the world's largest graphite production outside China, both essential for batteries and energy storage.
insights.speaker: Alberto Rizzi
insights.so_what: Brazil is positioned as a non-China source of battery materials for European supply chains.
insights.quote: The deal is instrumental in securing European access to Brazil’s critical minerals, including lithium and the world’s largest graphite production outside China.

themes.theme: China's grip on Brazilian green tech

insights.claim: China accounts for more than 89% of Brazil's solar-panel imports and provides much of the investment in Brazil's growing EV industry, while Chinese imports undercut Brazil's small photovoltaic sector.
insights.speaker: Alberto Rizzi
insights.so_what: Chinese dominance in Brazilian solar and EV supply chains is a competitive hurdle for EU firms.

insights.claim: If the EU and Brazil fail to deliver on Mercosur, China would gain the opening to entrench itself in the Brazilian economy with promises of investment and factories.
insights.speaker: Alberto Rizzi
insights.so_what: Mercosur failure would likely accelerate Chinese industrial FDI into Brazil.

insights.claim: European firms can build local supply chains and processing in Brazil while Chinese players often do only final assembly with their own inputs, giving Europe a value-added advantage.
insights.speaker: Alberto Rizzi
insights.so_what: Local-content-heavy EU investment models may be favoured by Brazilian policy.
insights.locator: European firms can build local supply chains

insights.claim: Brazil decided in February 2026 to raise the duty on EV assembly kits to 35% from January 2027, showing that increasing local value added is a key concern for Brasilia.
insights.speaker: Alberto Rizzi
insights.so_what: Higher duties on EV kits from January 2027 penalise assembly-only Chinese EV models in Brazil.

themes.theme: EU funding gap for Latin America

insights.claim: Despite rhetoric on Latin America's strategic value, the region received only a minor share of Global Gateway mobilised investment between 2021 and 2024, so the Global Europe Instrument in the 2028-2034 MFF should give Mercosur countries adequate resources.
insights.speaker: Alberto Rizzi
insights.so_what: Watch MFF 2028-2034 allocations as signal of EU commitment to Latin American investment.

insights.claim: Europeans should use diplomatic channels from capitals such as Rome and Madrid to signal that the EU offers Brazil the best return on investment despite more upfront conditionality than China.
insights.speaker: Alberto Rizzi
insights.so_what: Southern European capitals may lead EU economic diplomacy with Brazil.
